summary: Specifies three ways to carry Common Indexing Protocol requests, responses and index objects, using TCP, email and HTTP.

eli5.summary: Three delivery methods for index lists: a direct phone line, a mailed letter, or the web.

subtitle: Three ways to carry Common Indexing Protocol messages: a plain TCP text stream, ordinary email, or HTTP POST.

tldr.problem: The Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) passes MIME-formatted requests, replies and index objects between servers, but something has to actually carry those messages across the network.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2653 defines three transports: a text protocol over TCP with numbered response codes, the Internet mail infrastructure with a CIP-Version header and a mandatory Reply-To header, and HTTP using the POST method.
tldr.outcome: A CIP server can pick the transport that suits it, from a full TCP stream down to a leaf server that is little more than a database and an indexing program sending mail.

today: RFC 2653 is a Proposed Standard from August 1999, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It belongs to a family with RFC 2651 (architecture), RFC 2652 (MIME objects) and RFC 2654 (tagged index object).

sections.title: Philosophy and Conventions
sections.content:
RFC 2653 specifies three protocols for transporting CIP requests, responses and index objects, using TCP, mail and HTTP. The objects themselves are defined in RFC 2652 and the overall CIP architecture in RFC 2651. This document is the authoritative definition of the message formats and transfer mechanisms used over those three transports.

The design philosophy is building blocks. Instead of bulky protocol definition tools or ad-hoc text encodings, CIP draws on existing Internet technologies such as MIME, RFC-822, Whois++, FTP and SMTP, in the hope of easing implementation and consensus building.

The server that starts a connection is called the sender-CIP. The server that accepts the connection and answers is the receiver-CIP. In examples, octets from the sender are marked >>> and octets from the receiver <<< .
sections.eli5: CIP does not invent new tools. It reuses mail, web and file-transfer ideas that already work, like building with blocks you already own.

sections.title: Stream Transport and Version Check
sections.content:
Over TCP, CIP messages travel on a bidirectional connection as a simple text protocol. The connection can use any TCP port, as set by the mesh configuration. There is no well known port for CIP, so all configuration must include both a hostname and a port.

To stay compatible with existing Whois++ servers, a CIPv3 sender MUST first check that the newer protocol is supported. It sends the deliberately illegal Whois++ system command # CIP-Version: 3. A server that only speaks version 1 or 2 answers with a 500-series code and closes the connection. A CIPv3 server MUST instead answer with code 300. Future versions can be negotiated the same way with a different string, such as CIP-Version: 4.

If the sender can safely assume the server speaks CIPv3, it may send the version string and the request back to back, skipping the round trip. After a failed negotiation, the sender may retry with version 1 or 2 and may cache the result to avoid later attempts.
sections.eli5: Before sharing a secret handshake, you first ask whether the other kid knows it. If they look confused, you fall back to the old handshake.

sections.title: Message Format on the Stream
sections.content:
Once the version is confirmed, the sender transmits the request as a MIME message with Mime-Version and Content-Type headers only, with the network standard line ending CRLF. The request body format comes from the MIME object definitions, and the grammar is given in ABNF. A response is a three-digit code plus a comment, optionally followed by MIME headers and a body, and optionally an index object.

Messages end with SMTP-style termination. Data is sent octet for octet, except that when the pattern CR LF followed by one or more periods and CR LF appears, one more period is added. The sender then transmits CR LF, a period, CR LF to mark the end. The receiver reverses the change and reads everything up to, but not including, the terminator.

After answering, the receiver MUST get ready to read another request, resetting state to the point just after the version check. If the sender closes the connection, the receiver MUST abort reading the message and reset its state completely for a new sender.

The worked example in the RFC uses the tagged index object from RFC 2654 to send a datachanged command followed by an incremental index update.
sections.eli5: A line with only a dot means the message is over. If a real line would look like that, you add an extra dot so nobody stops reading too early.

sections.title: Response Codes
sections.content:
Every sender action, including requests, connection start and connection end, is acknowledged by the receiver with a response code. The receiver replies from the 200, 400 or 500 series, and the RFC lists what the sender should do for each code.

  • 200: request received and processed, no output follows. 201: processed, and a reply follows, ended by the SMTP-style delimiter.
  • 220 is the initial server banner and 222 says the connection is closing in response to the sender closing.
  • 300 accepts the requested CIP version.
  • 400: temporarily unable to process, retry later. It can mean the server lacks resources to accept an index.
  • 500 to 502: bad MIME format, unknown or missing request, or missing required CIP attributes. The sender should retry with a corrected message.
  • 520: connection aborted for an unexpected reason, so alert the local administrator.
  • 530, 531 and 532 cover a required signature, an invalid signature, and a signature that cannot be checked.
sections.eli5: Each answer is like a traffic light with a number. Some say go on, some say try again later, and some say tell a grown-up something is wrong.

sections.title: Mail as a Transport
sections.content:
CIP transactions can also use the Internet mail infrastructure. The RFC gives two motivations. It lowers the barrier for leaf servers, which only send index objects and can then be as little as a database and an indexing program with no full TCP implementation. It also fits the philosophy of reusing existing Internet technology, since MIME messages are suitable for mail by definition.

Because a mail message carries no version information in the MIME part, requests sent by mail MUST include a CIP-Version header line, in the form CIP-Version: number[.number].

Mail has no implicit return path, so CIP solves it by fiat: requests MUST include a Reply-To header as specified by RFC-822. A CIP server receiving mail without one MUST ignore it and should log a message for the local administrator. The receiver MUST NOT reply with an error to any address derived from the incoming mail. A sender that never wants a response can set Reply-To to <>, which receivers MUST never reply to. The RFC says turning off error reporting this way is generally a bad idea, but may be a fine simplification for a simple index pushing program.
sections.eli5: Sending by mail is like writing a letter. Since there is no phone line back, you must write your return address on it, or nobody will answer.

sections.title: HTTP as a Transport
sections.content:
HTTP MAY also carry CIP objects, since they are MIME objects. A transaction uses the POST method to send an application/index.cmd and returns an application/index.response or application/index.obj in the HTTP reply. The target URL is a configuration parameter of the relationship between sender and receiver.

The RFC's example posts an application/index.cmd.noop request and gets back HTTP/1.1 204 No Content.

Other HTTP features MAY be useful. A client can use Accept-Charset and Accept-Language to ask for a character set or natural language, Accept-Encoding to signal it can handle compressed responses, and If-Modified-Since to avoid wasted transmission of an unchanged index. A server can use Retry-After to ask the client to come back when it is less busy.
sections.eli5: Because the web already knows how to ask for things and say come back later, CIP can just ride along on web requests.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Index information can be protected at two levels: with the technology for securing MIME objects (RFC 1847), and by securing the transport itself.

For transport, the stream transport can be protected with TLS. For HTTP, security comes from Basic Authentication (RFC 2616), Digest Authentication (RFC 2617) or SSL/TLS. Extra protection for the mail exchange can come from Secure SMTP over TLS (RFC 2487).
sections.eli5: You can lock the letter itself, or lock the mailbox it travels in. CIP lets you do either one or both.
